blocks.text: **Cushing syndrome** is a clinical disorder resulting from prolonged exposure of body tissues to excessive glucocorticoids, particularly cortisol, irrespective of the underlying cause.
It results in metabolic, cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, dermatological, reproductive and neuropsychiatric complications.
**Cushing disease** is a specific subtype of Cushing syndrome caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.

items.text: Cushing syndrome: any cause of chronic glucocorticoid excess.
Ectopic ACTH syndrome: excessive ACTH production by a non-pituitary tumour.
Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome: caused by therapeutic glucocorticoid exposure.

blocks.text: Cushing syndrome is classified according to whether cortisol excess is ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent.
ACTH stimulates the adrenal glands to produce excessive cortisol.
Examples of ectopic ACTH-producing tumours include small-cell lung carcinoma, bronchial carcinoid tumours and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.
Excess cortisol production occurs independently of ACTH stimulation.

There is no universally accepted numerical severity grading system for Cushing syndrome. Severity is assessed according to cortisol excess, clinical complications and the presence of life-threatening manifestations.

blocks.text: **Important:** In severe endogenous Cushing syndrome, infection may present subtly because cortisol excess suppresses inflammatory responses. Maintain a low threshold for investigating infection.
Treatment depends on the source of excess cortisol.
First-line: transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. Medical therapy or radiotherapy is considered for persistent, recurrent or inoperable disease.

**Treatment selection pearl:** When rapid reduction of cortisol is required, steroidogenesis inhibitors are generally preferred. Metyrapone and osilodrostat have relatively rapid onset, while IV etomidate is an option in critical illness.
Paediatric Cushing syndrome is uncommon and should be managed by a paediatric endocrinologist.
The most important cause in children is often exogenous glucocorticoid exposure, although endogenous pituitary and adrenal tumours also occur.
There are no universally established routine paediatric dosing regimens for most medications used to treat endogenous Cushing syndrome.
**Do not simply apply adult doses to children or calculate doses using adult mg/kg assumptions.**
Growth, pubertal development, adrenal reserve and long-term skeletal health require particular attention.
For medicines without an established paediatric weight-based regimen, do not create a dose by extrapolating adult treatment ranges.
In children requiring emergency cortisol reduction, the choice of medicine, infusion rate and monitoring frequency must be individualised by a specialist team.
